title: When Does AI Supervision Help? A Role-Aware Study of Network Fraud Decision Management with Blockchain Auditability

paper.title: When Does AI Supervision Help? A Role-Aware Study of Network Fraud Decision Management with Blockchain Auditability
paper.abstract: Abstract When does a second artificial intelligence (AI) component improve a primary network-fraud decision rather than add operational burden? Our results show that supervision is not inherently beneficial: under the evaluated role assignments and operating policies, additional fraud recovery is usually accompanied by enough legitimate-user blocking to worsen the overall error profile. We study this question through a role-aware Decider–Supervisor (DS) framework with blockchain auditability, evaluating four directional configurations that combine centralised machine learning, a Federated Averaging (FedAvg)-trained federated meta-model, and Base or Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) large language model variants. The analysis compares primary-only and supervised decisions using non-hard fraud performance, intervention burden, paired uncertainty, conditional threshold calibration, traffic-mix and Review -capacity sensitivity, dependability tests, and blockchain lifecycle controls. The deterministic hard gate resolves 89.994% of fraudulent requests, so the primary AI analysis focuses on the remaining non-hard population. Conditional validation calibration does not produce a consistently transferable supervisory advantage on deployment replay. Among the predefined supervised configurations, DS-3 QLoRA is the least disruptive, but it still underperforms its primary FedAvg stage in F1 and total errors. Across 36 reweighted traffic mixtures, supervision reduces total errors only for DS-4 Base in two extreme high-fraud scenarios. Blockchain tests support digest verification, tamper detection, authorisation, single-use review resolution, and post-finalisation integrity, while exposing a pre-finalisation single-write limitation. These findings show that the value of AI supervision depends on role assignment, conditional calibration, escalation policy, traffic composition, and lifecycle controls rather than on the presence of a second model alone.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: As telecommunication systems evolve towards the highly distributed architectures envisioned for 6G, networked services will increasingly depend on scalable, privacy-preserving, and trustworthy coordination across heterogeneous computing and communication domains ( Valdez-Solis et al., 2026 ) . Telecom fraud remains difficult to detect because fraudsters may act cooperatively and conceal their activities within large populations of legitimate users, which limits the effectiveness of methods that assess users in isolation ( Wu et al., 2024 ) . Severe class imbalance in telecom-fraud datasets can bias learning towards the legitimate majority and reduce sensitivity to the comparatively rare fraud class ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . Centralised and federated learning (FL) have both been applied to network-intrusion detection, with experimental comparisons revealing distinct performance and scalability profiles across the two approaches ( Belenguer et al., 2023 ) . Federated intrusion-detection systems support collaborative model training without centralising raw local data, but non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data and privacy protection remain important deployment considerations ( Singh et al., 2024 ) . Related privacy-preserving federated-learning research also highlights statistical and model heterogeneity and communication overheads across distributed clients ( Han et al., 2026 ) . Large language models (LLMs) add language-generation and reasoning capabilities to such systems, but they can also produce plausible yet factually incorrect outputs with unwarranted confidence, raising concerns about uncertainty representation and reliability in consequential applications ( Shorinwa et al., 2025 ) . Recent network-security research increasingly treats intrusion detection as one stage of a broader mitigation and response pipeline rather than as an isolated classification task ( Mhamdi and Isa, 2024 ) . In 5G and beyond, intrusion-response selection must balance security effectiveness against quality-of-service impacts and the monetary, time, and energy costs of countermeasures ( Bozorgchenani et al., 2024 ) . A related trade-off arises at the detector level, where the operating threshold affects both attack detection and false alarms and, consequently, the volume of traffic subjected to blocking or further intervention ( Racherla et al., 2024 ) . Trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) should be assessed at the system level, where AI models operate as components of broader software systems whose trustworthiness must be considered across the software lifecycle ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Operationalising this view requires multidimensional evaluation strategies and quantitative metrics spanning the machine-learning lifecycle ( Kemmerzell et al., 2025 ) . Research on human–AI decision making also shows that adding another decision maker does not necessarily improve outcomes: on average, human–AI systems performed worse than the better-performing standalone human or AI system, with particularly negative results in decision-making tasks ( Vaccaro et al., 2024 ) . Blockchain is increasingly used in intrusion-detection systems as a decentralised trust and audit layer that supports tamper-evident recording, distributed coordination, and smart-contract-based policy enforcement ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . In secure FL, blockchain has also been combined with consensus-based model verification, transparent participation mechanisms, and personalised differential privacy to improve resilience against poisoning attacks while protecting client information ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . Nevertheless, blockchain-integrated deep-learning intrusion detection in industrial-control settings still lacks mature end-to-end integration and comprehensive evaluation of overall system effectiveness ( Devi Priya et al., 2025 ) . Centralised–federated comparisons in network-intrusion detection mainly examine detector performance and scalability ( Belenguer et al., 2023 ) , while federated intrusion-detection studies also address training-stage issues such as non-IID data and privacy protection ( Singh et al., 2024 ) . Work on trustworthy AI broadens evaluation to the software-system lifecycle ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , and blockchain-integrated intrusion-detection research points to gaps in end-to-end integration and system-level evaluation ( Devi Priya et al., 2025 ) . Existing studies do not yet explain how heterogeneous AI components should cooperate after inference, how predefined role directions affect final decisions, or when additional fraud recovery justifies legitimate-request blocking and Review workload. We examine these questions through a unified evaluation of decision quality, intervention burden, dependability, and blockchain-supported lifecycle enforcement. Our companion study introduced a blockchain-linked decision-management pipeline that transformed heterogeneous AI risk outputs into policy-resolved telecom/Internet of Things (IoT) fraud-control actions and recorded the resulting decision lifecycle ( Changizi et al., 2026 ) . The study treated its AI components as independent risk sources and did not evaluate them as cooperating components with asymmetric operational responsibilities. The present study reuses the centralised-ML, Federated Averaging (FedAvg)-trained federated meta-model, and LLM outputs and validation-derived thresholds from the companion pipeline without retraining the detectors. It then evaluates their downstream behaviour within the decision pipeline under explicitly assigned Decider and Supervisor roles. The proposed framework evaluates four directional configurations under a conservative escalation policy, in which a Decider produces the primary approve/block outcome and a Supervisor reassesses a bounded subset of primary approvals. The evaluation covers incremental fraud recovery and legitimate-request burden, sensitivity to traffic composition and finite Review capacity, dependability under controlled faults and score manipulation, and blockchain-supported submission, resolution, finalisation, and authorisation controls. The main contributions of this paper are as follows. • We formulate network-fraud decision management as a role-aware Decider–Supervisor (DS) problem and evaluate four configurations, DS-1–DS-4, spanning centralised-ML–LLM and FedAvg–LLM pairings in both implemented role directions. This shifts evaluation from isolated detector performance to complete role-aware decision pipelines. • We define bounded supervisory intervention through explicit candidacy, evidence-validity, no-downgrade, threshold, and resolution constraints. Its effects are measured relative to the primary-only stage through incremental fraud recovery, false-positive burden, recall, legitimate-request blocking, total errors, Review workload, and block-rate changes. • We evaluate operational sensitivity across Base and Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) LLM variants, binary and three-way Review interpretations, 36 exact traffic mixtures, and 11 finite Review -capacity levels. The analysis includes matched score-transfer auditing, label-free queue prioritisation, Pareto-frontier analysis, and normalised cost-ratio sensitivity. Oracle adjudication and cost ratios are used only as analytical bounds, not as deployable reviewer performance or empirically estimated operator costs. • We combine a formal threat-and-fault model with controlled dependability tests covering threshold and resolver sensitivity, unavailable Supervisor evidence, systematic and targeted score manipulation, LLM parsing and fallback faults, and alternative primary-component failure-resolution policies. • We integrate resolved decisions with a blockchain audit and enforcement layer and test digest reconstruction, payload tampering, conflicting or repeated submissions, Review resolution, finalisation, post-finalisation mutation, and endpoint authorisation. The evaluation reports both the enforced protections and the identified pre-finalisation single-write limitation without treating blockchain as a source of predictive performance. The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work and positions the research gap. Sections 3 and 4 define the system model and present the proposed framework. Section 5 describes the experimental design, followed by the results in Section 6 and their discussion in Section 7 . Section 8 addresses threats to validity and limitations, and Section 9 concludes the paper.

sections.text: The present study builds on two earlier studies by the authors ( Changizi et al., 2025 ; Changizi et al., 2026 ) but addresses a different research question. Table 1 makes the reuse boundary and the additional contribution explicit. Elements reused directly from the companion study, including the dataset, preprocessing pipeline, component outputs, validation-derived operating artefacts, and blockchain-linked components, are treated as fixed inputs rather than as new contributions of the present paper. The contribution examined here is the behaviour of those retained components when they are assigned asymmetric Decider and Supervisor responsibilities and evaluated through intervention burden, conditional operating behaviour, directional uncertainty, dependability, and blockchain-supported decision-lifecycle controls. sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Recent telecom-fraud work has focused on two recurring problems: relationships among users that are missed by isolated analysis and severe class imbalance. Latent synergy graph learning models cooperative fraudsters who disguise their activities within large populations of benign telecom users ( Wu et al., 2024 ) . Cost-sensitive graph attention has also been used to reduce majority-class bias and improve the classification of minority fraud cases ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . In both cases, the evaluation is centred on the predictive performance of a standalone detector. Federated learning offers an alternative to centralised network-intrusion detection when traffic data are distributed across organisations or devices. A direct comparison of centralised and FedAvg-based intrusion-detection models examined detection performance and scalability under the same experimental setting ( Belenguer et al., 2023 ) . Federated intrusion detection for next-generation networks has also been evaluated under privacy, class-imbalance, and non-IID data constraints ( Singh et al., 2024 ) . Work on personalised FL further addresses statistical and model heterogeneity, privacy protection, and communication bottlenecks across distributed clients ( Han et al., 2026 ) . FL has also been applied to transaction-fraud detection through a joint horizontal and vertical framework designed to improve fraud detection while addressing privacy protection and communication costs during collaborative training ( Li et al., 2026 ) . These studies focus on model training, distributed optimisation, privacy, heterogeneity, and detector performance. Some network-security work moves beyond detection to consider response and mitigation. One study embedded a hybrid deep-autoencoder–random-forest detector in a three-layer software-defined networking (SDN) framework for intrusion prevention and attack mitigation ( Mhamdi and Isa, 2024 ) . The evaluation included false-positive rate (FPR), controller throughput, and latency, covering both detection performance and controller overhead. Another study framed countermeasure selection in 5G and beyond as a trade-off between security and quality of service (QoS) ( Bozorgchenani et al., 2024 ) . The selection process considered security benefit together with monetary cost, preparation and deployment time, and energy consumption. These studies extend evaluation beyond classification accuracy to mitigation effectiveness, system overhead, and response cost. Threshold selection provides another link between detector output and operational action. In real-time IoT intrusion detection, the operating threshold affects both attack detection and false alarms and determines how much traffic is classified as non-benign and blocked ( Racherla et al., 2024 ) . This operational concern is consistent with a software-engineering view of trustworthy AI in which the model is evaluated as part of a wider AI-enabled system rather than in isolation ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Work on trustworthy AI also treats explainability as one contributor to trustworthiness alongside fairness, robustness, interpretability, and related properties ( Ali et al., 2023 ) . Trustworthiness evaluation therefore needs to cover multiple dimensions and use quantitative, domain-appropriate metrics across the machine-learning lifecycle ( Kemmerzell et al., 2025 ) . System quality depends on both model accuracy and the policy that converts model outputs into operational decisions. Adding a second decision maker cannot be assumed to improve an initial decision. Research on human–AI interaction in safety-critical industries distinguishes the roles assigned to AI-enabled systems and identifies AI output, usage context, and measurement choices as central dimensions for characterising and evaluating the interaction ( Bach et al., 2024 ) . Human–AI combinations have, on average, performed worse than the better-performing standalone human or AI system, with particularly negative results in decision-making tasks ( Vaccaro et al., 2024 ) . Human–AI collaboration is not equivalent to cooperation between two AI components, so these findings do not predict how an AI Supervisor will behave. Even so, the evidence cautions against assuming that a second decision maker will improve decision quality. The value of secondary review needs to be assessed through the decisions changed, the additional correct interventions achieved, and the new errors introduced. Related work on selective prediction, learning to defer, and classifier cascades provides a formal perspective on when a second decision stage should be invoked. Learning-to-defer formulations allow a model to pass selected decisions to a downstream decision maker while accounting for the downstream agent’s performance ( Madras et al., 2018 ) , and subsequent work jointly models prediction and deferral through a classifier and rejector under a cost-sensitive formulation ( Mozannar and Sontag, 2020 ) . Classification with a reject option similarly treats abstention as a cost-sensitive mechanism for avoiding risky misclassification ( Charoenphakdee et al., 2021 ) . In classifier cascades, confidence-based deferral can also be suboptimal when the downstream model has input-specific strengths or when the operating distribution changes ( Jitkrittum et al., 2023 ) . These approaches motivate selective rather than unconditional secondary intervention. The present study differs in that it does not learn a deferral policy or optimise a new classifier–rejector pair. Instead, it evaluates predefined AI–AI Decider–Supervisor configurations in which candidacy, evidence validity, operating thresholds, and resolution rules determine whether an existing secondary component can alter an existing primary decision. Secure federated-learning work mainly focuses on protecting distributed model training and aggregation. Verifiable differential privacy has been combined with Byzantine-resilient FL through secondary servers that validate model updates before verifiable differential-privacy noise is added during aggregation ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Model-contrastive FL has also addressed poisoning attacks, lightweight privacy preservation, and non-IID data heterogeneity within local optimisation and secure aggregation ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Blockchain-based FL has been combined with a proof-of-verification consensus protocol, personalised differential privacy, and a transparent reward mechanism ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . In federated intrusion detection, blockchain-based trust management, smart-contract verification, and trust-weighted aggregation have been used to support secure collaborative model construction ( Kamran et al., 2026 ) . A separate trust-aware federated intrusion-detection system combines differential-privacy evaluation, Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM)-based robustness assessment, trust-weighted aggregation, and a monitoring-only trust ledger that records client participation and trust scores throughout training ( Alshammari et al., 2026 ) . These approaches focus on local updates, client participation, privacy, aggregation, and global-model construction. They do not examine how trained-model scores or classifications are subsequently reviewed and converted into operational decisions. Blockchain-based intrusion-detection research covers a wider range of integrity, provenance, and coordination functions. A recent survey organises this literature into trusted-rule, machine-learning, deep-learning, and federated-learning paradigms ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Across these settings, blockchain supports tamper-evident records, provenance for model and training artefacts, decentralised coordination, and smart-contract-based enforcement of encoded rules and policies. A review of blockchain-integrated deep-learning intrusion detection in industrial-control systems reports limited end-to-end integration, insufficient assessment of overall system effectiveness, and unresolved issues involving scalability, latency, interoperability, computational complexity, and resource consumption ( Devi Priya et al., 2025 ) . These capabilities strengthen integrity and auditability, but they do not by themselves establish that a recorded decision was accurate, proportionate, or operationally appropriate. Our earlier study combined machine learning, LLMs, and blockchain within a heterogeneous telecom-fraud framework ( Changizi et al., 2025 ) . It showed that these technologies could operate within the same fraud-analysis architecture and evaluated six configurations with different distributions of decision authority between ML and LLM components. Some configurations already used threshold-based override, consultation, or fallback logic. However, the study did not formalise these interactions as a unified DS framework, isolate the effect of supervision against a primary-only baseline, or measure the intervention burden and new errors introduced by supervisory changes. The companion study moved from heterogeneous risk generation to blockchain-linked decision management for telecom/IoT fraud-control requests ( Changizi et al., 2026 ) . Alternative AI risk-source configurations were converted into policy-resolved operational actions, and the request-level lifecycle was recorded through a shared blockchain-linked audit and execution layer. The framework separated risk generation, policy resolution, and lifecycle recording, but the AI configurations remained alternative risk sources within that process. They were not evaluated as Decider and Supervisor components with asymmetric responsibilities. The study did not compare the implemented role directions or isolate the additional fraud recovery, false positives, legitimate-request blocking, and Review burden produced by selective supervisory intervention. The studies reviewed above address detector performance and distributed training ( Belenguer et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2024 ) , operational response and system-level trustworthiness ( Bozorgchenani et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Vaccaro et al., 2024 ) , and blockchain-supported auditability ( Devi Priya et al., 2025 ; Changizi et al., 2026 ) through separate evaluation settings. Even the closest prior architectures did not isolate supervisory effects against a primary-only baseline or evaluate directional role configurations together with intervention burden, finite Review capacity, dependability testing, and blockchain-supported lifecycle enforcement ( Changizi et al., 2025 ; Changizi et al., 2026 ) . The remaining question is how final decisions vary when a centralised-ML or FedAvg-based component is paired with an LLM in assigned DS roles, when selective supervision improves the primary decision, and whether any additional fraud recovery justifies the accompanying false positives, legitimate-request blocking, and Review workload. These effects also need to be examined across traffic compositions and finite Review capacities, under controlled faults and score manipulation, and alongside blockchain-supported controls over the downstream decision lifecycle. The framework presented in this paper evaluates centralised-ML–LLM and FedAvg–LLM configurations in both implemented role directions under a shared conservative escalation policy. The focus is on role assignment, intervention effects, operational sensitivity, dependability, and blockchain-supported lifecycle enforcement; training another standalone fraud detector is outside the study scope. sections.heading: 3 System Model and Problem Definition
sections.text: This section defines the network-fraud decision setting used in this study. The aim is to compare fraud-decision behaviour across predefined role assignments involving machine-learning, federated-learning, and large-language-model components under a conservative supervisory policy. The analysis focuses on predictive performance and on the measured error burden introduced by supervision, particularly false-positive inflation and legitimate-user blocking.

sections.heading: 3.1 Network-Fraud Decision Setting
sections.text: The system receives a stream of network requests. Each request is represented by a feature vector and associated metadata. For request i i , the input instance is denoted by x i x_{i} , and the system produces a binary operational decision: a i ∈ { APPROVE , BLOCK } . a_{i}\in\{\mathrm{APPROVE},\mathrm{BLOCK}\}. The ground-truth label is denoted by y i y_{i} , where y i = 1 y_{i}=1 represents a fraudulent request and y i = 0 y_{i}=0 represents a legitimate request. A correct block of a fraudulent request is counted as a true positive. An incorrect block of a legitimate request is counted as a false positive. In this setting, false negatives leave fraud unblocked, while false positives constitute a legitimate-user blocking burden by denying legitimate requests. The decision problem involves a trade-off between fraud detection and legitimate-user preservation. A model may achieve high recall by blocking many requests, but such behaviour can be undesirable if it produces excessive legitimate-user blocking. For that reason, the evaluation uses fraud-oriented metrics, such as recall and F1 score, together with operational metrics, such as FPR and block rate.

sections.heading: 3.2 Decider–Supervisor Role Model
sections.text: Each configuration consists of two role-specific components: a Decider and a Supervisor. The Decider produces the primary operational action, while the Supervisor is permitted to evaluate only eligible primary approvals. Primary blocks are protected by a no-downgrade rule and are therefore not reconsidered by the Supervisor. For request i i , let h i ∈ { 0 , 1 } h_{i}\in\{0,1\} denote the shared hard-fraud gate, where h i = 1 h_{i}=1 represents an explicit hard-fraud condition. For requests not locked by the hard-fraud gate, the Decider produces the primary action a i P ∈ { APPROVE , BLOCK } . a_{i}^{\mathrm{P}}\in\{\mathrm{APPROVE},\mathrm{BLOCK}\}. A primary approval becomes a candidate for supervisory evaluation only when it also satisfies the eligibility conditions of the selected role configuration. Let η i ∈ { 0 , 1 } \eta_{i}\in\{0,1\} denote the role-specific eligibility indicator. The supervisory candidate flag is defined as γ i = 𝟙 { h i = 0 } 𝟙 { a i P = APPROVE } η i . \gamma_{i}=\mathbb{1}\{h_{i}=0\}\mathbb{1}\{a_{i}^{\mathrm{P}}=\mathrm{APPROVE}\}\eta_{i}. (1) The indicator η i \eta_{i} represents the configuration-specific candidacy contract derived from the aligned role artefacts; no single universal feature rule is used. In DS-1, it requires LLM eligibility for a non-hard centralised-ML approval; in DS-2, no additional secondary eligibility condition is imposed beyond a non-hard LLM approval; in DS-3, it requires LLM eligibility for a valid non-hard FedAvg approval; and in DS-4, it additionally requires admissible LLM-primary evidence, including successful parsing and absence of fallback output, together with the FedAvg supervisor-candidate artefact. Consequently, η i \eta_{i} may depend on role-specific artefact metadata as well as the selected configuration and LLM variant. For a supervisory candidate, let e i ∈ { 0 , 1 } e_{i}\in\{0,1\} denote the configuration-specific evidence-availability indicator exported by the aligned secondary-component artefact. This indicator represents more than the physical presence of an output. Depending on the selected configuration, it may also incorporate component eligibility, successful LLM parsing, absence of fallback output, Phase-1 evidence availability, and valid probability and confidence ranges, where applicable. Let r i ∈ { 0 , 1 } r_{i}\in\{0,1\} denote the policy-stage evidence-validity condition. For LLM Supervisors, this condition rechecks successful parsing, absence of fallback output, and finite risk and confidence values. For the centralised-ML Supervisor in DS-2, it requires a finite probability value; the probability-implied confidence is retained as audit metadata and is not used as an activation condition. For the FedAvg Supervisor in DS-4, finite probability and confidence values are required. These policy-stage checks are applied defensively even when part of the same validation has already been performed while constructing the Phase-2 availability artefact. (2) In the exported artefacts, both the Supervisor-reliability state and the Supervisor-activation state encode u i u_{i} . The condition r i r_{i} captures the component-specific validity checks supported by the parse, fallback, probability, and confidence information, but is not retained as a separate lifecycle state. When activated, the Supervisor provides a risk score p i S ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] p_{i}^{\mathrm{S}}\in[0,1] . Let τ R S \tau_{\mathrm{R}}^{\mathrm{S}} and τ B S \tau_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{S}} denote the baseline-derived review and block thresholds, respectively, with τ R S ≤ τ B S \tau_{\mathrm{R}}^{\mathrm{S}}\leq\tau_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{S}} . The supervisory outcome is z i S ∈ { NI , RETAIN , REVIEW , BLOCK } , z_{i}^{\mathrm{S}}\in\{\mathrm{NI},\mathrm{RETAIN},\mathrm{REVIEW},\mathrm{BLOCK}\}, where NI \mathrm{NI} denotes the Not Invoked state. The outcome is defined as z i S = { NI , γ i = 0 , RETAIN , γ i = 1 ​ and ​ u i = 0 , RETAIN , u i = 1 ​ and ​ p i S < τ R S , REVIEW , u i = 1 ​ and ​ τ R S ≤ p i S < τ B S , BLOCK , u i = 1 ​ and ​ p i S ≥ τ B S . z_{i}^{\mathrm{S}}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{NI},&\gamma_{i}=0,\\[2.0pt] \mathrm{RETAIN},&\gamma_{i}=1\text{ and }u_{i}=0,\\[2.0pt] \mathrm{RETAIN},&u_{i}=1\text{ and }p_{i}^{\mathrm{S}}<\tau_{\mathrm{R}}^{\mathrm{S}},\\[2.0pt] \mathrm{REVIEW},&u_{i}=1\text{ and }\tau_{\mathrm{R}}^{\mathrm{S}}\leq p_{i}^{\mathrm{S}}<\tau_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{S}},\\[2.0pt] \mathrm{BLOCK},&u_{i}=1\text{ and }p_{i}^{\mathrm{S}}\geq\tau_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{S}}.\end{cases} (3) Thus, unavailable or unreliable supervisory evidence cannot alter the primary approval. Reliable evidence below the review threshold also retains the primary decision, whereas reliable evidence in the review or block region produces the corresponding escalation outcome. This role-aware formulation allows the same component family to be evaluated as a Decider in one configuration and as a Supervisor in another, while preserving a common supervisory lifecycle across the four configurations.

sections.heading: 3.3 Conservative Binary Decision Resolution
sections.text: The framework applies a conservative no-downgrade resolution policy. A primary block, including a block produced by the shared hard-fraud gate, cannot be converted into an approval by the Supervisor. For primary approvals, the final action depends on whether the Supervisor is invoked and, when activated, whether its reliable evidence produces a Retain , Review , or Block outcome. The implemented blockchain enforcement backend requires a binary final action and does not include a separate human-review outcome. Consequently, Review and Block remain distinct supervisory lifecycle states and are recorded separately in the audit metadata, but both are conservatively resolved as final blocks. By contrast, a Not Invoked or Retain outcome preserves the primary approval. For compact notation, let ℰ S = { REVIEW , BLOCK } \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{S}}=\{\mathrm{REVIEW},\mathrm{BLOCK}\} denote the supervisory escalation outcomes and let 𝒦 S = { NI , RETAIN } \mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{S}}=\{\mathrm{NI},\mathrm{RETAIN}\} denote the outcomes that preserve the primary approval. The final action is then defined as a i F = { BLOCK , a i P = BLOCK , BLOCK , a i P = APPROVE , z i S ∈ ℰ S , APPROVE , a i P = APPROVE , z i S ∈ 𝒦 S . a_{i}^{\mathrm{F}}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{BLOCK},&a_{i}^{\mathrm{P}}=\mathrm{BLOCK},\\[2.0pt] \mathrm{BLOCK},&a_{i}^{\mathrm{P}}=\mathrm{APPROVE},\ z_{i}^{\mathrm{S}}\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{S}},\\[2.0pt] \mathrm{APPROVE},&a_{i}^{\mathrm{P}}=\mathrm{APPROVE},\ z_{i}^{\mathrm{S}}\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{S}}.\end{cases} (4) The Review outcome is an audit-level escalation state, not a third final enforcement action. In a deployment containing a human-review or delayed-verification layer, this outcome could be resolved separately. In the present implementation, however, it is mapped to Block to preserve conservative fraud-control behaviour within the binary execution pathway. A decision-changing supervisory intervention occurs when the Decider initially approves a request but the final resolver converts that approval into a block. The row-level intervention indicator is defined as ι i = 𝟙 { a i P = APPROVE ∧ a i F = BLOCK } . \iota_{i}=\mathbb{1}\left\{a_{i}^{\mathrm{P}}=\mathrm{APPROVE}\land a_{i}^{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{BLOCK}\right\}. (5) Review-mediated and direct-block interventions are retained as separate lifecycle indicators: ι i R = 𝟙 { z i S = REVIEW } , ι i B = 𝟙 { z i S = BLOCK } . \iota_{i}^{\mathrm{R}}=\mathbb{1}\left\{z_{i}^{\mathrm{S}}=\mathrm{REVIEW}\right\},\qquad\iota_{i}^{\mathrm{B}}=\mathbb{1}\left\{z_{i}^{\mathrm{S}}=\mathrm{BLOCK}\right\}. (6) Under the current binary resolution policy, both escalation types change an eligible primary approval into a final block: ι i = ι i R + ι i B . \iota_{i}=\iota_{i}^{\mathrm{R}}+\iota_{i}^{\mathrm{B}}. This separation preserves the distinction between review-mediated blocking and direct supervisory blocking in the row-level lifecycle artefacts. Because both escalation outcomes become final blocks under the implemented binary resolver, the compact paper analysis reports their sum as the overall decision-changing intervention count. The separate indicators remain available for lifecycle inspection and audit, while the aggregate intervention measure captures their combined operational effect on fraud recall, legitimate false positives, and final block rate.

sections.heading: 3.4 Formal Threat and Fault Model
sections.text: The dependability evaluation distinguishes non-adversarial component faults from adversarial attempts to alter the decision or audit lifecycle. The protected assets include the primary decision, Supervisor evidence and score, supervisory candidate and intervention states, the resolved final action, the review-resolution state, exported decision payloads and digests, and the corresponding blockchain lifecycle records. The principal security and dependability properties are preservation of existing primary blocks, containment of unavailable or invalid supervisory evidence, deterministic resolution, authorised state modification, single-use review resolution, detection of exported-payload modification, lifecycle traceability, and protection of evaluated states after finalisation. The threat model considers request-side input manipulation, faulty or compromised primary and supervisory components, systematic and targeted Supervisor-score manipulation, authorised-but-faulty validators, unauthorised smart-contract callers, off-chain artefact modification, and faulty decision-resolution logic. The principal trust boundaries separate request submission, primary and secondary component outputs, policy-based resolution, exported audit artefacts, and blockchain-maintained request state. The evaluation assumes that the local blockchain and administrative account are not compromised, authorised-validator private keys are not stolen, the retained artefacts are accessible for offline evaluation, and ground-truth labels are used only for experimental assessment. Consensus-layer attacks, host compromise, denial-of-service, model-training privacy attacks, side-channel leakage, and validator-key theft are outside the scope of the present study. Each considered fault or threat is mapped to a controlled empirical assessment. These assessments include Supervisor-evidence unavailability, systematic score bias, targeted threshold-crossing manipulation, LLM parsing and fallback faults, primary-LLM output failure, exported-payload tampering, duplicate and conflicting decision submissions, repeated review resolution, post-finalisation mutation, and unauthorised state-changing contract calls. Support for a security or dependability property is limited to the tested component, endpoint, lifecycle state, and attacker-capability boundary. Any violation found in these tests is reported as a system limitation and is not obscured by aggregate fraud-detection performance.

sections.heading: 4 Proposed Role-Aware Decider–Supervisor Framework
sections.text: This section introduces the role-aware DS framework used in this study. The framework evaluates specified pairings of heterogeneous AI components, where one component produces the primary fraud decision and another component reviews selected risky approvals. The aim is to compare final fraud-decision behaviour, the measured error and legitimate-user blocking burden introduced by supervisory intervention, and blockchain-audited enforcement outcomes across the four implemented role-aware configurations. The framework is not a dynamic model-selection or adaptive orchestration system. It evaluates four role-aware configurations under a shared conservative resolution policy. This structure keeps the comparison focused on role assignment, supervisor type, and LLM variant. Routing and run-time model selection are outside the comparison.

sections.text: Fig. 1 presents the architecture that implements the formal decision model defined in Section 3 . It connects the shared hard-fraud gate, the assigned DS roles, role-specific candidacy and evidence checks, the conservative resolver, and the blockchain audit and enforcement layer. The figure distinguishes protected hard-gate and primary blocks from the supervisory pathway applied to eligible primary approvals. The configuration-specific role assignments are summarised in Table 3 , while the lifecycle variables and resolution rules follow the definitions given in Section 3 . Figure 1: Role-aware DS decision lifecycle. Solid arrows show the active non-hard primary-approval pathway, while dashed arrows show protected hard-gate and primary-block bypasses and non-activation branches. Only eligible primary approvals become supervisory candidates. An ineligible primary approval produces a Not Invoked state, whereas unavailable or unreliable supervisory evidence produces Retain . When supervision is activated, the secondary risk score is mapped to Retain , Review , or Block . For primary approvals, the conservative binary resolver preserves Not Invoked and Retain outcomes as approvals and maps both Review and Block outcomes to final blocks before blockchain audit and enforcement. The framework separates fraud-decision logic from audit recording. The Decider and Supervisor determine the final approve/block outcome, while the blockchain layer records the resolved decision and associated metadata. This separation is important because the study examines the effect of supervisory review on decision quality, without treating blockchain execution as the source of detection performance.

sections.heading: 4.3 Blockchain Audit and Enforcement Layer
sections.text: Once the final action has been resolved, the framework submits the decision record, lifecycle metadata, and retained data and model digests to the blockchain layer. The contract records the request state and governs the permitted review and finalisation transitions without altering the fraud decision itself. The integrity, lifecycle, authorisation, and execution tests are described in Section 5 .

sections.heading: 5 Experimental Design
sections.text: This section describes the data, reused component outputs, baseline-derived thresholds, evaluation metrics, operational-validation analyses, and dependability and blockchain tests used in the study.

sections.heading: 5.1 Dataset and Request Labels
sections.text: The present study reuses the dataset, preprocessing pipeline, standalone M1–M3 risk-source artefacts, blockchain-linked audit components, and centralised-ML, FedAvg-trained federated meta-model, and LLM-family outputs from the companion study ( Changizi et al., 2026 ) ; no detector is retrained. The standalone risk sources are denoted as M1 for centralised ML, M2 for the FedAvg-trained federated meta-model, and M3 for the LLM family. Throughout this paper, FedAvg refers to the FedAvg-trained federated meta-model reused from the companion pipeline. Each request is represented by a feature vector and associated metadata. Ground-truth labels distinguish fraudulent requests from legitimate requests, and the operational outcome is binary: Approve or Block . The reused data are synthetic and were generated by the project-specific data-generation pipeline provided with the companion-study reproducibility materials rather than collected from live network traffic. The training corpus comprises 27 controlled scenario instantiations spanning total anomaly rates of 10%, 15%, and 20% and soft-fraud shares from 20% to 100%, producing 27,000 records in total. The independent deployment corpus was generated separately as 100,000 requests from 1,000 synthetic users using a fixed generation seed of 777 and profile seed of 2024, with a 5% anomaly rate, 10% of anomalous requests assigned to soft fraud, and a moderate controlled-drift setting. The data-generation and preprocessing code, including the recorded generation parameters, is available through the companion GitLab repository identified in the Data and Code Availability statement. The raw deployment artefacts contain 100,000 request rows. For label-based predictive and supervisory-intervention evaluation, deployment outputs are aligned with the ground-truth file using the composite business key formed by the hashed identifier, asset hash, timestamp, and Ethereum address. This one-to-one alignment yields 99,996 unique labelled deployment requests after four duplicate-key rows are removed. The blockchain execution analysis instead retains the complete 100,000-row submission stream because it characterises transaction execution and audit overhead rather than label-based predictive performance. Consequently, small differences between the final action rates reported in the predictive tables and the blockchain summary arise from their different denominators and do not indicate inconsistent decision logic. Within the matched labelled deployment set, a soft-fraud request is defined as a fraudulent request that remains inside the admissible synthetic operating envelope and therefore does not activate the deterministic hard-fraud gate. Formally, soft fraud corresponds to y i = 1 y_{i}=1 and h i = 0 h_{i}=0 , whereas hard fraud corresponds to y i = 1 y_{i}=1 and h i = 1 h_{i}=1 . The labelled deployment evaluation contains 4,997 fraudulent requests, of which 4,497 are hard-fraud cases resolved by the deterministic gate and 500 are soft-fraud cases that remain available to the AI decision pipeline. Thus, 89.994% of all fraudulent requests are resolved by the hard gate before Decider–Supervisor intervention. The 500 soft-fraud requests comprise 166 single-component, 167 double-component, and 167 triple-component cases. Soft-fraud recall therefore measures detection performance on the fraudulent requests for which the evaluated AI decision components can affect the outcome.

sections.heading: 5.2 Role Assignment and Score-Transfer Audit
sections.text: Role assignments follow Table 3 and remain unchanged throughout each experiment; no dynamic routing or model selection is used. A matched score-transfer audit checks that the directional comparisons reuse the component evidence from the companion pipeline without recomputing scores for the alternative role direction. Requests are aligned using the canonical composite business key, and each comparison is restricted to requests for which the same component score is available in both implemented directions. Request-level scores are then compared using an absolute numerical tolerance of 1 × 10 − 12 1\times 10^{-12} . Ground-truth labels are not used to define the common support or assess score identity. The audit verifies score preservation on matched support, but not equal score availability, equivalent calibration, identical operating thresholds, or a causal effect of role assignment.

Primary Decider actions are unchanged, while Supervisor review and block thresholds are loaded from the baseline validation-policy artefacts and kept fixed for the main deployment replay. Labelled deployment outcomes are used only for performance assessment and do not determine these reported operating thresholds. In addition, a separate conditional-calibration sensitivity analysis re-estimates an escalation boundary using only the held-out validation requests that the Decider approves, satisfy the configuration-specific candidacy contract, have available Supervisor evidence, and contain a finite Supervisor score. This supplementary analysis is used to test whether the main findings can be explained solely by transferring thresholds from the standalone population to the conditional supervisory population; it does not replace the predefined operating policy. The centralised-ML and FedAvg Supervisors use the M1 and M2 thresholds, respectively. Because the centralised-ML and FedAvg Supervisors are unchanged across the two LLM-primary variants, their thresholds remain identical for Base and QLoRA. sections.heading: 5.4 Conditional Validation Calibration Sensitivity
sections.text: To assess whether threshold transfer from the standalone baselines explains the supervisory results, an additional validation-only calibration analysis is performed on the conditional supervisory population. For each configuration and LLM variant, calibration uses only validation requests for which the primary action is Approve , the configuration-specific candidate flag is active, Supervisor evidence is available, and the Supervisor score is finite. Candidate escalation thresholds are drawn from the observed conditional-validation scores, together with a no-intervention sentinel above the maximum observed score. Three prespecified validation rules are evaluated independently: a minimum-error rule that minimises total validation errors, a maximum-F1 rule that maximises validation F1, and a false-positive-budget rule requiring no more than 50 added false positives per recovered fraud case when such a point exists. These rules provide a favourable conditional operating test for supervision by selecting the escalation boundary on the exact validation subpopulation eligible for supervisory intervention rather than transferring the standalone-population threshold unchanged. Threshold selection uses validation data only. Each selected threshold is then frozen and replayed on the labelled deployment population without further optimisation. Because the implemented binary resolver maps both Review and Block escalation to a final block, the binary outcome identifies an escalation boundary but does not independently identify two deployment-optimal review and block thresholds. The inherited block threshold is therefore retained for lifecycle interpretation, while the conditional analysis is treated as a sensitivity analysis rather than a replacement operating policy.

sections.heading: 5.5 LLM Variants and Role Use
sections.text: Both Base and QLoRA variants are evaluated in every configuration. In DS-1 and DS-3, the LLM is the Supervisor, so the primary decision is unchanged across variants and any difference appears only after supervision. In DS-2 and DS-4, the LLM is the Decider; Base and QLoRA produce different primary profiles, while the same variant has the same primary output before the centralised-ML or FedAvg Supervisor is applied. These comparisons characterise the evaluated pipelines and do not attribute the results solely to QLoRA adaptation.

sections.heading: 5.6 Decision Stages
sections.text: Each configuration is evaluated before supervision using the primary decision a i P a_{i}^{\mathrm{P}} and after resolution using the final decision a i F a_{i}^{\mathrm{F}} , as defined in Section 3 . Their difference quantifies the change associated with supervision in the matched deployment replay. Review-mediated and direct-block escalations remain separate in the lifecycle records, although both lead to a final Block under the implemented binary resolver.

sections.text: The evaluation reports accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score using their standard binary-classification definitions, together with FPR, block rate, total errors, and soft-fraud recall. True positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN), and false negatives (FN) follow their standard binary-classification meanings. sections.heading: 5.9 Blockchain Evaluation Setup
sections.text: Blockchain execution is evaluated over the complete 100,000-row submission stream described above. The recorded lifecycle and contract controls follow the framework defined in Section 4 . The exported measures include final approval and block rates, average gas per transaction, mean and 95th-percentile end-to-end latency, measured throughput, validator participation rate, and Jain fairness index. The main results table reports the principal outcome-rate and execution-overhead measures, while the participation and fairness outputs remain available in the reproducibility artefacts.

sections.heading: 5.10 Reproducibility Artefacts
sections.text: The experimental pipeline exports the row-level decisions, lifecycle fields, comparison summaries, robustness outputs, blockchain test records, figures, and LaTeX tables used in the paper. Each artefact is indexed by decision stage, configuration, LLM variant, and experiment, allowing reported results to be traced to the corresponding source output. Tables and figures are generated from the exported files rather than assembled manually. The retained validation outputs also include the population-alignment and score-semantics checks, traffic-mix and Review -capacity results, score-transfer audit, Pareto and cost-sensitivity analyses, validation manifests, and hashed output inventory. Repository access is described in the Data and Code Availability statement.

sections.heading: 5.11 Operational Traffic-Mix and Review-Capacity Validation
sections.text: Operational sensitivity is evaluated over the matched population of 99,996 requests using the retained primary and final actions, candidacy states, Supervisor scores, thresholds, and resolver outputs. These request-level values remain unchanged throughout the analysis; only the assumed traffic composition or available Review capacity is varied. Traffic composition is varied through exact class-conditional reweighting. For each configuration and variant, block rates are estimated separately for legitimate, soft-fraud, and hard-fraud requests. Fraud prevalence takes values of 0.5%, 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, and 20%, while the soft-fraud share of the fraudulent population takes values of 0%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%. The resulting 36 scenarios preserve the measured class-conditional decision behaviour and report primary and final outcomes as rates and expected events per 100,000 requests. Labels are used to estimate these class-conditional outcomes, but not to alter thresholds or request-level decisions. Finite Review capacity is assessed by reconstructing the Review-band population from the retained Supervisor scores, lifecycle flags, and review and block thresholds. Candidates are ranked by decreasing Supervisor score, with the deterministic row identifier used to break ties. Labels are excluded from queue construction and ranking and are introduced only after selection to measure fraud yield, legitimate-request burden, severity composition, queue coverage, and captured queued fraud. The evaluated capacities are 0, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, and 2,500 requests per 100,000 deployment requests. The three-way analysis keeps Approve , Block , and unresolved Review separate and evaluates fail-open and fail-closed treatments of queue overflow. Perfect adjudication is reported only as an oracle upper bound for selected Review cases; it does not represent an implemented reviewer or measured human performance. The 16 primary and final operating points are also compared using Pareto dominance over false-negative and false-positive counts, with duplicate objective pairs collapsed before frontier construction. A supplementary resource-aware comparison includes selected Review volume. Normalised cost sensitivity uses C j = λ FN ​ FN j + FP j + λ R ​ R j , C_{j}=\lambda_{\mathrm{FN}}\mathrm{FN}_{j}+\mathrm{FP}_{j}+\lambda_{\mathrm{R}}R_{j}, (10) where the false-positive weight is fixed to one, λ FN \lambda_{\mathrm{FN}} is the assumed relative cost of a missed fraud case, λ R \lambda_{\mathrm{R}} is the assumed relative cost of selecting a Review case, and R j R_{j} is the selected Review volume. These ratios are analytical assumptions rather than estimated financial costs, and the corresponding break-even regions are reported separately from the oracle Review bounds.

sections.heading: 5.12 Dependability, Robustness, and Security Assessment
sections.text: All tests use the matched deployment replay and the frozen DS-1–DS-4 lifecycle artefacts; no model is retrained, no LLM inference is rerun, and no policy is retuned on the labelled deployment set. Request-sampling uncertainty is estimated using 10,000 paired stratified bootstrap replicates with 95% confidence intervals. Primary and final decisions remain paired, and resampling preserves the legitimate, soft-fraud, and hard-fraud stratum sizes. These intervals capture sampling variation within the fixed replay, not uncertainty from retraining, alternative random seeds, regenerated data, or new deployment environments. Policy sensitivity is examined by jointly shifting the baseline-derived Supervisor review and block thresholds from − 0.10 -0.10 to + 0.10 +0.10 around their reported values. The conservative resolver is also compared with a direct-block-only alternative, while a separate three-way interpretation leaves Review unresolved to measure queue volume and composition. Component faults cover Supervisor-evidence unavailability, LLM parsing and fallback failures, bounded Supervisor-score perturbations, and hypothetical primary-LLM failure-resolution strategies. Experiments that sample intermediate fault locations use 500 replicates per fault rate. Targeted score manipulation is evaluated under the K2-O oracle class-targeted profile, which assumes exact knowledge of the review threshold and target class. Bounded upward and downward shifts are applied only to eligible threshold-crossing cases while primary decisions, candidacy conditions, thresholds, and resolver logic remain unchanged. Labels are used only to construct class-specific worst-case evaluation sets, not as information available during ordinary operation. The test measures oracle-targeted threshold manipulation and does not establish general adversarial robustness. Blockchain security and lifecycle integrity are tested through digest reconstruction, controlled post-export payload modification, duplicate and conflicting initial-decision submissions, repeated review resolution and finalisation, post-finalisation state mutation, and unauthorised calls to recordAIDecision and resolveReview . Live tests use fresh deployments of the retained contract application binary interface (ABI) and bytecode. Duplicate submissions are sent as new Ethereum transactions with new account nonces, so they test application-level duplicate handling; replay of an identical signed transaction is not evaluated. Authorisation tests compare unauthorised calls with authorised-validator controls and inspect both transaction outcomes and request-state changes. sections.heading: 7 Discussion
sections.text: The results show that DS systems must be evaluated by their end-to-end operating profile rather than by the presence of a second model. The key issue is whether supervisory intervention recovers enough fraud to justify the resulting legitimate-user burden and Review workload.

sections.heading: 7.1 Are Supervisors Always Beneficial?
sections.text: On the complete matched population, no decision-changing Supervisor improves F1 or total errors relative to its corresponding primary-only stage. DS-1 Base adds 44 true positives but 29,182 false positives, while DS-3 Base adds 94 true positives but 38,542 false positives. The recall gains arise from broad escalation and do not indicate a better overall error profile. DS-1 Base is particularly unsuitable as an operational setting under the evaluated replay: supervision reduces accuracy to 55.13%, raises FPR to 47.18%, and blocks 49.78% of all requests. Such a profile would impose an excessive legitimate-request burden and should not be treated as a viable deployment operating point. Lower intervention rates produce less disruptive outcomes, but even the more selective pipelines do not outperform their primary-only baselines on F1 or total errors. Because no operator-specific cost model is estimated, these findings characterise the measured fraud-recovery and legitimate-user-blocking trade-offs; they do not establish economic net benefit.

sections.heading: 7.2 Why Base LLM Supervisors Can Be Over-Conservative
sections.text: The Base LLM Supervisors produce broad escalation under the baseline-derived thresholds and binary resolver. In DS-3 Base, the FedAvg primary stage has an F1 score of 71.64% and a FPR of 3.88%; after supervision, these become 18.94% and 44.45%, respectively. Because both reliable Review and Block outcomes become final blocks, broad supervisory signals directly amplify legitimate false positives. This does not show that Base LLMs are inherently unsuitable for supervision; it indicates that their score distributions require stricter candidacy, threshold, and resolver control in an enforcement-oriented pipeline.

sections.heading: 7.3 Base–QLoRA Differences When the LLM Is the Supervisor
sections.text: In DS-1 and DS-3, the evaluated QLoRA Supervisor is markedly more selective than the Base Supervisor within the corresponding role-aware configurations. In DS-3, QLoRA produces 304 interventions, adding four true positives and 300 false positives, compared with 38,636 interventions, 94 true positives, and 38,542 false positives for Base. Its final profile remains much closer to the FedAvg primary stage, with 95.87% accuracy, 97.08% recall, 70.12% F1, and a FPR of 4.20%. This difference should not be attributed causally to QLoRA adaptation alone because the variants retain their own realised artefacts, score distributions, and baseline-derived thresholds. DS-3 QLoRA also does not improve on the FedAvg primary stage overall: recall rises by 0.08 percentage points and soft recall by 0.80 percentage points, but F1 falls by 1.52 percentage points, FPR rises by 0.32 percentage points, and total errors increase by 296. The evidence supports a narrower conclusion: the evaluated QLoRA Supervisor is more controlled than the evaluated Base Supervisor under the tested pipeline.

sections.heading: 7.4 Role Assignment Matters
sections.text: The directional comparisons reflect complete implemented configurations and should not be interpreted as isolated causal role swaps. Each direction retains its role-specific candidacy, evidence-validity, threshold, and resolution conditions. The score-transfer audit confirms that retained component scores remain identical on pair-common support within the 1 × 10 − 12 1\times 10^{-12} tolerance, but it does not equalise score availability or the surrounding operating contracts. For the centralised-ML–LLM pair, both role directions produce decision-changing supervision, but their relative performance depends on the LLM variant. DS-2 has the stronger Base profile, whereas DS-1 has the stronger QLoRA profile. In DS-2, centralised-ML supervision increases fraud recall but introduces enough legitimate false positives to reduce F1 and increase total errors relative to the corresponding LLM-primary stage. For the FedAvg–LLM pair, DS-3 QLoRA has the highest F1 and lowest FPR among the supervised resolved configurations, although it remains weaker than its primary FedAvg stage. The reverse DS-4 QLoRA direction produces substantially lower F1 and higher FPR. Role-aware design must assess the complete pipeline. Strong performance as a Decider does not imply value as a Supervisor, and directional differences cannot be attributed to role labels alone.

sections.heading: 7.5 Dependability, Review Workload, and Failure Handling
sections.text: Bounded supervision does not guarantee better final decisions. Across the paired-bootstrap and local threshold-sensitivity analyses, every intervention-producing pipeline retains lower F1 and higher FPR than its corresponding primary-only stage. A direct-block-only resolver reduces the false-positive burden created by review-mediated escalation, but does not overturn the primary-stage comparison. Traffic-mix reweighting shows that these trade-offs depend on fraud prevalence and severity composition. Supervision reduces total errors only for DS-4 Base in two extreme scenarios combining 20% fraud prevalence with a 75% or 100% soft-fraud share. DS-2 Base achieves higher F1 in 14 of the 36 scenarios but does not reduce total errors in any scenario, while DS-2 QLoRA shows neither higher F1 nor fewer errors. Higher F1 can therefore occur without a reduction in incorrect decisions, and deployment claims must be conditioned on the expected traffic mix and the relative consequences of false positives and false negatives. Keeping Review unresolved transfers immediate blocking burden to a finite queue; it does not remove that burden. The smaller DS-1 QLoRA and DS-3 QLoRA queues fit within a capacity of 100 requests per 100,000, whereas the larger DS-2 and DS-4 queues remain dominated by legitimate requests. For DS-2 Base and QLoRA, the first 100 ranked requests capture only three of 19 and one of 17 queued fraud cases, respectively. In DS-4 QLoRA, the first 100 ranked requests contain no fraud, while the first 1,000 capture seven of eight queued fraud cases but also include 993 legitimate requests. These results describe queue composition and oracle bounds, not reviewer accuracy, delay, cost, or final adjudication. The Pareto and normalised cost-ratio analyses reinforce this trade-off. The DS-3 QLoRA final output recovers four additional fraud cases relative to the primary FedAvg output but introduces 300 additional legitimate blocks. With false-positive cost normalised to one and Review cost set to zero, it becomes lower-cost only when λ FN > 75 \lambda_{\mathrm{FN}}>75 . Recent industry evidence illustrates the economic scale of telecommunications fraud: TNS, drawing on the latest CFCA Fraud Loss Survey, reports that global telecommunications fraud losses increased from $38.95 billion in 2023 to $41.82 billion in 2025 ( Transaction Network Services, 2026 ) . However, such aggregate industry-loss estimates do not provide compatible per-request costs for a missed fraud case and an incorrectly blocked legitimate request, and therefore cannot establish that a 75:1 cost ratio is realistic for a particular operator. The value λ FN > 75 \lambda_{\mathrm{FN}}>75 should consequently be interpreted only as the measured break-even boundary of the normalised sensitivity analysis, not as an empirically supported telecom cost ratio. Complete Supervisor-evidence loss safely reproduces the primary-only decisions, but also removes incremental fraud recovery. Systematic score bias and K2-O targeted manipulation show that score provenance and threshold governance are equally important because eligible requests near intervention boundaries can be moved into or out of escalation. The K2-O result remains an oracle worst-case stress test and does not establish threshold-agnostic adversarial robustness. Primary-LLM failure is different because the primary action itself is unavailable. The fail-open, fail-closed, unresolved- Review , and DS-2 centralised-ML action-only takeover analyses are hypothetical policy sensitivities and do not represent implemented failover behaviour. Production use would require an authenticated failure signal, explicit authority transfer, complete secondary-evidence coverage, bounded Review capacity, and a tested recovery transition.

sections.heading: 7.6 Practical Implications for Network-Fraud Decision Management
sections.text: Deployment decisions should not be based on recall alone. FPR, block rate, false positives added, and FP per TP gain are needed to show whether additional fraud recovery is achieved through disproportionate blocking. Selective intervention is preferable to broad escalation, but even a low intervention rate can increase total errors. Each supervised pipeline should be compared with its own primary-only stage and assessed using operator-specific weights for missed fraud, legitimate-user blocking, Review workload, and service disruption. Role assignment is likewise an operational design choice and should be assessed at the complete-pipeline level rather than attributed to model families or role labels in isolation. Blockchain contributes auditability and lifecycle enforcement, not predictive quality. The tested contract records role and decision metadata, supports digest reconstruction, enforces authorisation for recordAIDecision and resolveReview , permits only one review resolution, and protects the tested states after finalisation. It does not provide universal pre-finalisation single-write protection because a conflicting initial-decision submission can alter the stored state before finalisation. Production deployment requires explicit duplicate or idempotency controls, broader endpoint testing, and stronger key-management protection.

sections.heading: 8 Threats to Validity and Limitations
sections.text: The principal interpretation boundaries concern the controlled synthetic evaluation setting, the predefined role and policy configurations, the evaluated LLM variants and failure-handling assumptions, and the scope of the blockchain implementation. These boundaries define the conditions under which the reported DS comparisons and lifecycle results should be interpreted.

sections.heading: 8.1 Dataset, Statistical Scope, and Generalisation
sections.text: The study reuses the controlled synthetic network-request corpus, labels, and component artefacts from the companion study. This common data representation and preprocessing support consistent comparison across DS-1–DS-4 and controlled analysis of hard/soft fraud, traffic composition, and supervisory intervention. The evaluation is nevertheless an offline synthetic replay rather than validation on live operator traffic. Soft fraud is design-specific and denotes labelled fraud that remains within the admissible synthetic envelope without activating the hard-fraud gate; the matched replay contains 500 such requests. The traffic-mix analysis varies fraud prevalence and the soft-fraud share while preserving the measured class-conditional behaviour, retained actions, thresholds, and within-class distributions. It therefore evaluates sensitivity to class composition rather than broader forms of distributional or behavioural shift. Similarly, the paired stratified bootstrap intervals quantify request-sampling uncertainty within the matched replay rather than uncertainty arising from alternative corpus generation, retraining, or deployment conditions. The findings should therefore be interpreted as evidence for the evaluated artefacts, thresholds, role configurations, and policies under the tested replay conditions. Validation on independently generated or operational datasets, repeated training runs, and prospective temporal evaluation would be needed to assess transfer to other deployment environments.

sections.heading: 8.2 Role, Policy, and Utility Scope
sections.text: The study evaluates four predefined DS pipelines in both implemented role directions. The comparisons therefore characterise the complete operating profiles produced by their role-specific candidacy, evidence, thresholds, and resolution rules rather than an isolated causal effect of exchanging Decider and Supervisor labels. The reported supervisory effects are conditional on the implemented no-downgrade binary resolver and the predefined baseline-derived thresholds. The direct-block-only and three-way Review analyses demonstrate how alternative resolution policies redistribute burden between immediate blocking and unresolved workload. The validation-only conditional-calibration analysis additionally tests whether transferring standalone thresholds explains the main results; although some selected operating points improve individual metrics, none reduces deployment total errors below the corresponding primary-only stage. The reported results therefore describe the tested policy and threshold configurations rather than all possible supervisory operating policies. The normalised cost analysis complements these comparisons by varying dimensionless relative weights assigned to false negatives, false positives, and selected Review cases. These weights are analytical rather than operator-derived and are used to identify break-even regions, not to claim a universal economic optimum. Operator-specific deployment decisions would require empirical loss, service-level, and review-cost information.

sections.heading: 8.3 LLM Variant and Failure-Handling Scope
sections.text: The experiments compare one evaluated Base LLM variant with one QLoRA-adapted variant under the retained artefacts, baseline-derived thresholds, and role-aware decision policies. In DS-1 and DS-3, the QLoRA Supervisor is more selective and less disruptive than Base, whereas in DS-2 and DS-4 the Base–QLoRA differences already arise at the primary stage. These results therefore characterise the evaluated variants and complete pipelines rather than an isolated causal effect of QLoRA adaptation. The DS-2 and DS-4 lifecycle artefacts do not implement a run-time authority-transfer mechanism for unavailable primary-LLM output. The reported fail-open, fail-closed, unresolved- Review , and DS-2 centralised-ML takeover results are therefore post hoc policy sensitivities rather than implemented failover behaviour. In particular, DS-4 does not provide FedAvg evidence for the original LLM-block population, so a complete FedAvg takeover cannot be evaluated.

sections.heading: 8.4 Blockchain Execution and Integrity Scope
sections.text: The blockchain layer is evaluated as a local audit and lifecycle-enforcement backend rather than a production-scale blockchain benchmark. At the observed average execution costs of 1,154,200–1,189,698 gas per transaction, individually recording 100,000 requests corresponds to approximately 115.42–118.97 billion gas, or about 3,847–3,966 full-block equivalents when 30 million gas per block is used solely as an illustrative capacity benchmark. A production-oriented architecture could instead retain request-level records off-chain and periodically anchor batch commitments, such as Merkle roots, on-chain; the illustrative anchoring counts reported in this study describe batching frequency only, because Merkle construction, proof verification, anchoring cost, latency, and storage savings were not implemented or measured. The original Ganache state used for Phase-4 execution was not retained, so the integrity analysis combines digest reconstruction of the retained artefacts with lifecycle tests on fresh deployments of the retained contract ABI and bytecode. The duplicate-submission tests assess application-level handling through new Ethereum transactions rather than replay of an identical signed transaction. Before finalisation, identical and conflicting initial-decision submissions can be accepted, and a conflicting submission can alter the stored request state. By contrast, repeated review resolution, repeated finalisation, and the tested post-finalisation mutations are rejected. The contract therefore does not provide universal pre-finalisation single-write protection or general replay resistance. The authorisation tests cover recordAIDecision and resolveReview on fresh local deployments. Unauthorised calls to these endpoints revert without changing request state, while the corresponding authorised controls succeed. These results establish the tested lifecycle and authorisation properties within the evaluated local implementation; broader endpoint and adversary coverage remains outside the tested boundary.

sections.heading: 9 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: This paper presented a role-aware DS framework for network-fraud decision management with blockchain auditability. Four predefined configurations assigned centralised ML, a FedAvg-trained federated meta-model, and LLM-family components to Decider and Supervisor roles under a shared conservative resolution policy. The framework formalised bounded supervisory intervention through candidacy, evidence-validity, no-downgrade, threshold, and resolution constraints and evaluated complete pipelines using predictive, intervention-burden, unresolved- Review , dependability, and blockchain-integrity measures. The results show that supervision is not inherently beneficial. Base LLM Supervisors recover limited additional fraud in DS-1 and DS-3 while introducing substantial false-positive burden. DS-3 QLoRA has the highest F1 and lowest FPR among the supervised resolved configurations, but remains weaker than its primary FedAvg stage in F1, legitimate-user preservation, and total errors. Directional differences between DS-1 and DS-2 and between DS-3 and DS-4 characterise complete role-specific configurations and do not isolate the causal effect of exchanging the role labels. The operational analyses further show that these conclusions depend on traffic composition, resolver design, Review capacity, and relative error costs. Across 36 exactly reweighted traffic mixtures, supervision reduces total errors only for DS-4 Base in the two scenarios combining 20% fraud prevalence with a 75% or 100% soft-fraud share. Leaving Review unresolved reduces immediate automated blocking but transfers the burden into a finite queue. The DS-1 QLoRA and DS-3 QLoRA queues fit within a capacity of 100 requests per 100,000, whereas the larger DS-2 and DS-4 queues are overwhelmingly legitimate and require substantially greater capacity for complete processing. Under the normalised cost model, the DS-3 QLoRA final output becomes lower-cost than the primary FedAvg output only when λ FN > 75 \lambda_{\mathrm{FN}}>75 ; this is an analytical break-even boundary, not an empirically estimated operator cost. Complete Supervisor-evidence loss safely reproduces the primary decisions, but systematic score bias and K2-O targeted threshold-crossing manipulation can sharply alter intervention outcomes. The queue-capacity and K2-O results are analytical oracle bounds; they do not represent measured reviewer performance or establish threshold-agnostic adversarial robustness. Primary-LLM failure likewise remains dependent on hypothetical fail-open, fail-closed, unresolved- Review , or takeover policies because no run-time authority-transfer contract is implemented. The blockchain layer provides auditability and lifecycle enforcement without contributing predictive performance. Digest reconstruction confirms the internal consistency of the retained artefacts, and recomputation detects every tested nonzero payload modification. Repeated review resolution, repeated finalisation, and the tested post-finalisation mutations are rejected. Unauthorised calls to recordAIDecision and resolveReview also revert without changing request state, while the corresponding authorised-validator controls succeed. However, identical and conflicting initial-decision submissions can be accepted before finalisation, including a conflicting submission that changes the stored request state. The supported protections are specific to the tested endpoints, callers, lifecycle states, and local deployment. Future work will implement the unresolved- Review pathway as a live bounded service with authenticated queue admission, explicit capacity and overflow rules, measurable delay and resource use, and measured post-review outcomes. It will also examine broader LLM architectures, prompts, adaptation and calibration procedures, independently generated and operational datasets, repeated training runs, temporal drift, and threshold-agnostic adversarial strategies. Production-oriented failure handling will require authenticated primary-failure signals, complete secondary-evidence coverage, explicit authority transfer, bounded unresolved-request handling, and tested recovery to normal operation. The smart-contract lifecycle will additionally require pre-finalisation single-write or idempotency controls, broader endpoint and role-governance testing, validator-key protection, compromised-authorised-actor scenarios, alternative consensus settings, and evaluation under production network conditions.

The companion GitLab repository contains the shared dataset-construction pipeline, standalone M1–M3 risk-source artefacts, and blockchain-linked audit components reused in this study. The present-paper GitLab repository contains the role-aware DS evaluation notebooks, DS-1–DS-4 result files, generated figures and LaTeX tables, intervention and directional-comparison analyses, matched score-transfer audits, conditional-validation calibration analyses, paired-bootstrap uncertainty and policy-sensitivity outputs, component-failure and hypothetical primary-LLM failure-resolution analyses, and blockchain audit, digest-reconstruction, tamper-detection, and lifecycle-test artefacts. It also includes the operational-validation materials for population alignment, probability provenance, traffic-mix reweighting, finite Review capacity, label-free queue ranking, overflow policies, Pareto and normalised cost-ratio analyses, oracle bounds, validation manifests, the figure registry, and the hashed output inventory.
