A Role-Aware Study of Network Fraud Decision Management with Blockchain Auditability Journal: Journal of Network and Computer Applications Saviz Changizi Email: s.changizi@surrey.ac.uk Corresponding author: Corresponding author Address: 6G Innovation Centre, Institute for Communication Systems, University of Surrey, Guildford, United Kingdom Nasibeh Mohammadzadeh Email: nasibeh.m@gmail.com Address: Department of Network Engineering, Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (UPC), Barcelona, Spain Mohammad Shojafar Email: m.shojafar@surrey.ac.uk Address: 6G Innovation Centre, Institute for Communication Systems, University of Surrey, Guildford, United Kingdom Rahim Tafazolli Email: r.tafazolli@surrey.ac.uk Address: 6G Innovation Centre, Institute for Communication Systems, University of Surrey, Guildford, United Kingdom Abstract When does a second artificial intelligence (AI) component improve a primary network-fraud decision rather than add operational burden? Our results show that supervision is not inherently beneficial: under the evaluated role assignments and operating policies, additional fraud recovery is usually accompanied by enough legitimate-user blocking to worsen the overall error profile. We study this question through a role-aware Decider–Supervisor (DS) framework with blockchain auditability, evaluating four directional configurations that combine centralised machine learning, a Federated Averaging (FedAvg)-trained federated meta-model, and Base or Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) large language model variants. The analysis compares primary-only and supervised decisions using non-hard fraud performance, intervention burden, paired uncertainty, conditional threshold calibration, traffic-mix and Review -capacity sensitivity, dependability tests, and blockchain lifecycle controls. The deterministic hard gate resolves 89.994% of fraudulent requests, so the primary AI analysis focuses on the remaining non-hard population. Conditional validation calibration does not produce a consistently transferable supervisory advantage on deployment replay. Among the predefined supervised configurations, DS-3 QLoRA is the least disruptive, but it still underperforms its primary FedAvg stage in F1 and total errors. Across 36 reweighted traffic mixtures, supervision reduces total errors only for DS-4 Base in two extreme high-fraud scenarios. Blockchain tests support digest verification, tamper detection, authorisation, single-use review resolution, and post-finalisation integrity, while exposing a pre-finalisation single-write limitation. These findings show that the value of AI supervision depends on role assignment, conditional calibration, escalation policy, traffic composition, and lifecycle controls rather than on the presence of a second model alone. Keywords: Network fraud decision management , Decider–Supervisor framework , trustworthy AI , AI dependability , federated learning , large language models , blockchain auditability 1 Introduction As telecommunication systems evolve towards the highly distributed architectures envisioned for 6G, networked services will increasingly depend on scalable, privacy-preserving, and trustworthy coordination across heterogeneous computing and communication domains ( Valdez-Solis et al., 2026 ) . Telecom fraud remains difficult to detect because fraudsters may act cooperatively and conceal their activities within large populations of legitimate users, which limits the effectiveness of methods that assess users in isolation ( Wu et al., 2024 ) . Severe class imbalance in telecom-fraud datasets can bias learning towards the legitimate majority and reduce sensitivity to the comparatively rare fraud class ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . Centralised and federated learning (FL) have both been applied to network-intrusion detection, with experimental comparisons revealing distinct performance and scalability profiles across the two approaches ( Belenguer et al., 2023 ) . Federated intrusion-detection systems support collaborative model training without centralising raw local data, but non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data and privacy protection remain important deployment considerations ( Singh et al., 2024 ) . Related privacy-preserving federated-learning research also highlights statistical and model heterogeneity and communication overheads across distributed clients ( Han et al., 2026 ) . Large language models (LLMs) add language-generation and reasoning capabilities to such systems, but they can also produce plausible yet factually incorrect outputs with unwarranted confidence, raising concerns about uncertainty representation and reliability in consequential applications ( Shorinwa et al., 2025 ) . Recent network-security research increasingly treats intrusion detection as one stage of a broader mitigation and response pipeline rather than as an isolated classification task ( Mhamdi and Isa, 2024 ) . In 5G and beyond, intrusion-response selection must balance security effectiveness against quality-of-service impacts and the monetary, time, and energy costs of countermeasures ( Bozorgchenani et al., 2024 ) . A related trade-off arises at the detector level, where the operating threshold affects both attack detection and false alarms and, consequently, the volume of traffic subjected to blocking or further intervention ( Racherla et al., 2024 ) . Trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) should be assessed at the system level, where AI models operate as components of broader software systems whose trustworthiness must be considered across the software lifecycle ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Operationalising this view requires multidimensional evaluation strategies and quantitative metrics spanning the machine-learning lifecycle ( Kemmerzell et al., 2025 ) . Research on human–AI decision making also shows that adding another decision maker does not necessarily improve outcomes: on average, human–AI systems performed worse than the better-performing standalone human or AI system, with particularly negative results in decision-making tasks ( Vaccaro et al., 2024 ) . Blockchain is increasingly used in intrusion-detection systems as a decentralised trust and audit layer that supports tamper-evident recording, distributed coordination, and smart-contract-based policy enforcement ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . In secure FL, blockchain has also been combined with consensus-based model verification, transparent participation mechanisms, and personalised differential privacy to improve resilience against poisoning attacks while protecting client information ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . Nevertheless, blockchain-integrated deep-learning intrusion detection in industrial-control settings still lacks mature end-to-end integration and comprehensive evaluation of overall system effectiveness ( Devi Priya et al., 2025 ) . Centralised–federated comparisons in network-intrusion detection mainly examine detector performance and scalability ( Belenguer et al., 2023 ) , while federated intrusion-detection studies also address training-stage issues such as non-IID data and privacy protection ( Singh et al., 2024 ) . Work on trustworthy AI broadens evaluation to the software-system lifecycle ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , and blockchain-integrated intrusion-detection research points to gaps in end-to-end integration and system-level evaluation ( Devi Priya et al., 2025 ) . Existing studies do not yet explain how heterogeneous AI components should cooperate after inference, how predefined role directions affect final decisions, or when additional fraud recovery justifies legitimate-request blocking and Review workload. We examine these questions through a unified evaluation of decision quality, intervention burden, dependability, and blockchain-supported lifecycle enforcement. Our companion study introduced a blockchain-linked decision-management pipeline that transformed heterogeneous AI risk outputs into policy-resolved telecom/Internet of Things (IoT) fraud-control actions and recorded the resulting decision lifecycle ( Changizi et al., 2026 ) . The study treated its AI components as independent risk sources and did not evaluate them as cooperating components with asymmetric operational responsibilities. The present study reuses the centralised-ML, Federated Averaging (FedAvg)-trained federated meta-model, and LLM outputs and validation-derived thresholds from the companion pipeline without retraining the detectors. It then evaluates their downstream behaviour within the decision pipeline under explicitly assigned Decider and Supervisor roles. The proposed framework evaluates four directional configurations under a conservative escalation policy, in which a Decider produces the primary approve/block outcome and a Supervisor reassesses a bounded subset of primary approvals. The evaluation covers incremental fraud recovery and legitimate-request burden, sensitivity to traffic composition and finite Review capacity, dependability under controlled faults and score manipulation, and blockchain-supported submission, resolution, finalisation, and authorisation controls. The main contributions of this paper are as follows. • We formulate network-fraud decision management as a role-aware Decider–Supervisor (DS) problem and evaluate four configurations, DS-1–DS-4, spanning centralised-ML–LLM and FedAvg–LLM pairings in both implemented role directions. This shifts evaluation from isolated detector performance to complete role-aware decision pipelines. • We define bounded supervisory intervention through explicit candidacy, evidence-validity, no-downgrade, threshold, and resolution constraints. Its effects are measured relative to the primary-only stage through incremental fraud recovery, false-positive burden, recall, legitimate-request blocking, total errors, Review workload, and block-rate changes. • We evaluate operational sensitivity across Base and Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) LLM variants, binary and three-way Review interpretations, 36 exact traffic mixtures, and 11 finite Review -capacity levels. The analysis includes matched score-transfer auditing, label-free queue prioritisation, Pareto-frontier analysis, and normalised cost-ratio sensitivity. Oracle adjudication and cost ratios are used only as analytical bounds, not as deployable reviewer performance or empirically estimated operator costs. • We combine a formal threat-and-fault model with controlled dependability tests covering threshold and resolver sensitivity, unavailable Supervisor evidence, systematic and targeted score manipulation, LLM parsing and fallback faults, and alternative primary-component failure-resolution policies. • We integrate resolved decisions with a blockchain audit and enforcement layer and test digest reconstruction, payload tampering, conflicting or repeated submissions, Review resolution, finalisation, post-finalisation mutation, and endpoint authorisation. The evaluation reports both the enforced protections and the identified pre-finalisation single-write limitation without treating blockchain as a source of predictive performance. The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work and positions the research gap. Sections 3 and 4 define the system model and present the proposed framework. Section 5 describes the experimental design, followed by the results in Section 6 and their discussion in Section 7 . Section 8 addresses threats to validity and limitations, and Section 9 concludes the paper. 1.1 Relationship to Prior Work by the Authors The present study builds on two earlier studies by the authors ( Changizi et al., 2025 ; Changizi et al., 2026 ) but addresses a different research question. Table 1 makes the reuse boundary and the additional contribution explicit. Elements reused directly from the companion study, including the dataset, preprocessing pipeline, component outputs, validation-derived operating artefacts, and blockchain-linked components, are treated as fixed inputs rather than as new contributions of the present paper. The contribution examined here is the behaviour of those retained components when they are assigned asymmetric Decider and Supervisor responsibilities and evaluated through intervention burden, conditional operating behaviour, directional uncertainty, dependability, and blockchain-supported decision-lifecycle controls. Table 1: Relationship between the present study and prior work by the authors. Study Research question Reused elements New elements in that study Principal conclusion HPCC 2025 ( Changizi et al., 2025 ) How can heterogeneous ML, LLM, and blockchain components be combined within telecom-fraud analysis configurations? Conceptual precedent for heterogeneous ML–LLM–blockchain integration and for distributing decision authority between ML and LLM components; no HPCC dataset or trained detector is directly reused in the present study. Six heterogeneous configurations with different distributions of ML/LLM decision authority, including threshold-based override, consultation, and fallback behaviour. Heterogeneous AI and blockchain components can be integrated within alternative fraud-analysis architectures, but supervisory effects relative to a common primary-only baseline were not isolated. Companion study ( Changizi et al., 2026 ) How can heterogeneous AI risk outputs be converted into auditable operational telecom/IoT fraud-control decisions? Dataset and preprocessing pipeline, standalone M1–M3 outputs, validation-derived operating artefacts, and blockchain-linked audit components reused directly by the present study. Standalone M1–M3 risk-source artefacts, policy-resolved decision management, and a shared blockchain-linked audit and execution lifecycle. Heterogeneous risk sources can be converted into policy-resolved actions and recorded through a common auditable lifecycle, without assigning the AI components asymmetric Decider–Supervisor roles. Present study When does a second AI component improve or degrade a primary fraud decision under assigned Decider–Supervisor roles? Dataset, preprocessing, standalone M1–M3 outputs, validation-derived baseline thresholds, and blockchain-linked audit components from the companion pipeline; no detector retraining. Four directional DS configurations; primary-versus-supervised intervention analysis; non-hard population analysis; conditional-validation calibration sensitivity; paired directional uncertainty; Review-capacity and traffic-mix analyses; controlled fault and score-manipulation tests; and blockchain lifecycle-security assessment. Supervision is not inherently beneficial: its value depends on role assignment, conditional threshold behaviour, intervention burden, resolver policy, traffic composition, and lifecycle controls. 2 Related Work Recent telecom-fraud work has focused on two recurring problems: relationships among users that are missed by isolated analysis and severe class imbalance. Latent synergy graph learning models cooperative fraudsters who disguise their activities within large populations of benign telecom users ( Wu et al., 2024 ) . Cost-sensitive graph attention has also been used to reduce majority-class bias and improve the classification of minority fraud cases ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . In both cases, the evaluation is centred on the predictive performance of a standalone detector. Federated learning offers an alternative to centralised network-intrusion detection when traffic data are distributed across organisations or devices. A direct comparison of centralised and FedAvg-based intrusion-detection models examined detection performance and scalability under the same experimental setting ( Belenguer et al., 2023 ) . Federated intrusion detection for next-generation networks has also been evaluated under privacy, class-imbalance, and non-IID data constraints ( Singh et al., 2024 ) . Work on personalised FL further addresses statistical and model heterogeneity, privacy protection, and communication bottlenecks across distributed clients ( Han et al., 2026 ) . FL has also been applied to transaction-fraud detection through a joint horizontal and vertical framework designed to improve fraud detection while addressing privacy protection and communication costs during collaborative training ( Li et al., 2026 ) . These studies focus on model training, distributed optimisation, privacy, heterogeneity, and detector performance. Some network-security work moves beyond detection to consider response and mitigation. One study embedded a hybrid deep-autoencoder–random-forest detector in a three-layer software-defined networking (SDN) framework for intrusion prevention and attack mitigation ( Mhamdi and Isa, 2024 ) . The evaluation included false-positive rate (FPR), controller throughput, and latency, covering both detection performance and controller overhead. Another study framed countermeasure selection in 5G and beyond as a trade-off between security and quality of service (QoS) ( Bozorgchenani et al., 2024 ) . The selection process considered security benefit together with monetary cost, preparation and deployment time, and energy consumption. These studies extend evaluation beyond classification accuracy to mitigation effectiveness, system overhead, and response cost. Threshold selection provides another link between detector output and operational action. In real-time IoT intrusion detection, the operating threshold affects both attack detection and false alarms and determines how much traffic is classified as non-benign and blocked ( Racherla et al., 2024 ) . This operational concern is consistent with a software-engineering view of trustworthy AI in which the model is evaluated as part of a wider AI-enabled system rather than in isolation ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Work on trustworthy AI also treats explainability as one contributor to trustworthiness alongside fairness, robustness, interpretability, and related properties ( Ali et al., 2023 ) . Trustworthiness evaluation therefore needs to cover multiple dimensions and use quantitative, domain-appropriate metrics across the machine-learning lifecycle ( Kemmerzell et al., 2025 ) . System quality depends on both model accuracy and the policy that converts model outputs into operational decisions. Adding a second decision maker cannot be assumed to improve an initial decision. Research on human–AI interaction in safety-critical industries distinguishes the roles assigned to AI-enabled systems and identifies AI output, usage context, and measurement choices as central dimensions for characterising and evaluating the interaction ( Bach et al., 2024 ) . Human–AI combinations have, on average, performed worse than the better-performing standalone human or AI system, with particularly negative results in decision-making tasks ( Vaccaro et al., 2024 ) . Human–AI collaboration is not equivalent to cooperation between two AI components, so these findings do not predict how an AI Supervisor will behave. Even so, the evidence cautions against assuming that a second decision maker will improve decision quality. The value of secondary review needs to be assessed through the decisions changed, the additional correct interventions achieved, and the new errors introduced. Related work on selective prediction, learning to defer, and classifier cascades provides a formal perspective on when a second decision stage should be invoked. Learning-to-defer formulations allow a model to pass selected decisions to a downstream decision maker while accounting for the downstream agent’s performance ( Madras et al., 2018 ) , and subsequent work jointly models prediction and deferral through a classifier and rejector under a cost-sensitive formulation ( Mozannar and Sontag, 2020 ) . Classification with a reject option similarly treats abstention as a cost-sensitive mechanism for avoiding risky misclassification ( Charoenphakdee et al., 2021 ) . In classifier cascades, confidence-based deferral can also be suboptimal when the downstream model has input-specific strengths or when the operating distribution changes ( Jitkrittum et al., 2023 ) . These approaches motivate selective rather than unconditional secondary intervention. The present study differs in that it does not learn a deferral policy or optimise a new classifier–rejector pair. Instead, it evaluates predefined AI–AI Decider–Supervisor configurations in which candidacy, evidence validity, operating thresholds, and resolution rules determine whether an existing secondary component can alter an existing primary decision. Secure federated-learning work mainly focuses on protecting distributed model training and aggregation. Verifiable differential privacy has been combined with Byzantine-resilient FL through secondary servers that validate model updates before verifiable differential-privacy noise is added during aggregation ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Model-contrastive FL has also addressed poisoning attacks, lightweight privacy preservation, and non-IID data heterogeneity within local optimisation and secure aggregation ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Blockchain-based FL has been combined with a proof-of-verification consensus protocol, personalised differential privacy, and a transparent reward mechanism ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . In federated intrusion detection, blockchain-based trust management, smart-contract verification, and trust-weighted aggregation have been used to support secure collaborative model construction ( Kamran et al., 2026 ) . A separate trust-aware federated intrusion-detection system combines differential-privacy evaluation, Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM)-based robustness assessment, trust-weighted aggregation, and a monitoring-only trust ledger that records client participation and trust scores throughout training ( Alshammari et al., 2026 ) . These approaches focus on local updates, client participation, privacy, aggregation, and global-model construction. They do not examine how trained-model scores or classifications are subsequently reviewed and converted into operational decisions. Blockchain-based intrusion-detection research covers a wider range of integrity, provenance, and coordination functions. A recent survey organises this literature into trusted-rule, machine-learning, deep-learning, and federated-learning paradigms ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Across these settings, blockchain supports tamper-evident records, provenance for model and training artefacts, decentralised coordination, and smart-contract-based enforcement of encoded rules and policies. A review of blockchain-integrated deep-learning intrusion detection in industrial-control systems reports limited end-to-end integration, insufficient assessment of overall system effectiveness, and unresolved issues involving scalability, latency, interoperability, computational complexity, and resource consumption ( Devi Priya et al., 2025 ) . These capabilities strengthen integrity and auditability, but they do not by themselves establish that a recorded decision was accurate, proportionate, or operationally appropriate. Our earlier study combined machine learning, LLMs, and blockchain within a heterogeneous telecom-fraud framework ( Changizi et al., 2025 ) . It showed that these technologies could operate within the same fraud-analysis architecture and evaluated six configurations with different distributions of decision authority between ML and LLM components. Some configurations already used threshold-based override, consultation, or fallback logic. However, the study did not formalise these interactions as a unified DS framework, isolate the effect of supervision against a primary-only baseline, or measure the intervention burden and new errors introduced by supervisory changes. The companion study moved from heterogeneous risk generation to blockchain-linked decision management for telecom/IoT fraud-control requests ( Changizi et al., 2026 ) . Alternative AI risk-source configurations were converted into policy-resolved operational actions, and the request-level lifecycle was recorded through a shared blockchain-linked audit and execution layer. The framework separated risk generation, policy resolution, and lifecycle recording, but the AI configurations remained alternative risk sources within that process. They were not evaluated as Decider and Supervisor components with asymmetric responsibilities. The study did not compare the implemented role directions or isolate the additional fraud recovery, false positives, legitimate-request blocking, and Review burden produced by selective supervisory intervention. The studies reviewed above address detector performance and distributed training ( Belenguer et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2024 ) , operational response and system-level trustworthiness ( Bozorgchenani et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Vaccaro et al., 2024 ) , and blockchain-supported auditability ( Devi Priya et al., 2025 ; Changizi et al., 2026 ) through separate evaluation settings. Even the closest prior architectures did not isolate supervisory effects against a primary-only baseline or evaluate directional role configurations together with intervention burden, finite Review capacity, dependability testing, and blockchain-supported lifecycle enforcement ( Changizi et al., 2025 ; Changizi et al., 2026 ) . The remaining question is how final decisions vary when a centralised-ML or FedAvg-based component is paired with an LLM in assigned DS roles, when selective supervision improves the primary decision, and whether any additional fraud recovery justifies the accompanying false positives, legitimate-request blocking, and Review workload. These effects also need to be examined across traffic compositions and finite Review capacities, under controlled faults and score manipulation, and alongside blockchain-supported controls over the downstream decision lifecycle. The framework presented in this paper evaluates centralised-ML–LLM and FedAvg–LLM configurations in both implemented role directions under a shared conservative escalation policy. The aim is to compare fraud-decision behaviour across predefined role assignments involving machine-learning, federated-learning, and large-language-model components under a conservative supervisory policy. The analysis focuses on predictive performance and on the measured error burden introduced by supervision, particularly false-positive inflation and legitimate-user blocking. 3.1 Network-Fraud Decision Setting The system receives a stream of network requests. Each request is represented by a feature vector and associated metadata. For request i i , the input instance is denoted by x i x_{i} , and the system produces a binary operational decision: a i ∈ { APPROVE , BLOCK } . a_{i}\in\{\mathrm{APPROVE},\mathrm{BLOCK}\}. The ground-truth label is denoted by y i y_{i} , where y i = 1 y_{i}=1 represents a fraudulent request and y i = 0 y_{i}=0 represents a legitimate request. A correct block of a fraudulent request is counted as a true positive. An incorrect block of a legitimate request is counted as a false positive. In this setting, false negatives leave fraud unblocked, while false positives constitute a legitimate-user blocking burden by denying legitimate requests. The decision problem involves a trade-off between fraud detection and legitimate-user preservation. A model may achieve high recall by blocking many requests, but such behaviour can be undesirable if it produces excessive legitimate-user blocking. For that reason, the evaluation uses fraud-oriented metrics, such as recall and F1 score, together with operational metrics, such as FPR and block rate. 3.2 Decider–Supervisor Role Model Each configuration consists of two role-specific components: a Decider and a Supervisor. The protected assets include the primary decision, Supervisor evidence and score, supervisory candidate and intervention states, the resolved final action, the review-resolution state, exported decision payloads and digests, and the corresponding blockchain lifecycle records. The principal security and dependability properties are preservation of existing primary blocks, containment of unavailable or invalid supervisory evidence, deterministic resolution, authorised state modification, single-use review resolution, detection of exported-payload modification, lifecycle traceability, and protection of evaluated states after finalisation.
